title: Ten families to know
teaches: The signatures of ten flowering-plant families that make up much of what grows in a temperate field or garden, and how to tell grasses, sedges and rushes apart

blocks.text: Experienced botanists rarely start a key at couplet 1. They glance at a plant and know its family, and then use the family's own key, which is far shorter. Knowing families is the shortcut, and fewer of them matter than you might think. There are over 400 families of flowering plants, but in a meadow, a hedgerow or a garden in a temperate country, one with warm summers and cold winters, a handful of them make up most of what you see.

Each family has a **signature**, a few features that go together. No one feature is enough: plenty of plants have five petals. But five petals with many stamens, toothed leaves and a pair of small flaps, called stipules, where each leaf joins the stem says rose family, and is usually right.

blocks.caption: Ten families, each by its signature. Drawn simply.

blocks.text: The **rose** family gives most of the fruit in a temperate orchard: apples, pears, cherries, plums, strawberries, raspberries and blackberries. The **pea** family's flowers have a big upright petal, the banner, two side petals, the wings, and two joined at the bottom into a keel that hides the stamens; its seeds grow in pods, and its roots carry lesson 10's nitrogen-fixing bacteria. The **mint** family, with basil, sage, lavender and self-heal (one of lesson K2's drawn plants), has square stems you can feel by rolling one between your fingers, opposite leaves and two-lipped flowers, and usually a smell when a leaf is rubbed.

The **aster** family, with sunflowers, daisies, dandelions and lettuce, is one of the two largest families of flowering plants, with about 30,000 species.[^orchids] What looks like one flower is a head of dozens or hundreds: a sunflower's face is a central disc of tiny flowers, each making one seed, ringed by flowers that each grow one long petal. The **carrot** family carries its tiny flowers in umbrellas, called umbels, on hollow stems, and includes carrots, parsley, dill and celery, and some of the most poisonous plants there are (lesson K4).

The **mustard** family has six stamens, four long and two short (lesson K1's class for them), and its four petals in a cross gave it its old name, Cruciferae, the cross-bearers;[^old-names] lesson 20's cabbage white lives on it. The **buttercup** family has a knob of many separate carpels at the centre of each flower, and many of its members, including buttercups themselves, larkspurs and monkshood, are poisonous. The **heath** family, with blueberries, huckleberries, salal, rhododendrons and heather, hangs its flowers as little bells or urns and grows on acid soil with fungal partners in its roots; lesson 11's pinesap belongs to it.

Three families of grass-like plants grow in the same wet meadows and are easy to confuse. Roll the stem between your fingers. A **grass** stem is round and hollow, with solid joints along it. A **sedge** stem is usually solid and triangular, with three sharp edges. A **rush** stem is round and not hollow: it is filled with spongy pith. Botanists remember it by a rhyme: sedges have edges, rushes are round, grasses have joints all the way to the ground.

Grasses are worth knowing for their own sake. Wheat, rice, corn, barley, oats, sugar cane and bamboo are grasses, and rice, wheat and corn alone supply roughly half the calories people eat. Their flowers are tiny and green, wrapped in scales and grouped in spikelets, because they are pollinated by wind and have no animal to advertise to.

Strictly, that makes this a lesson of eleven families rather than ten, or ten groups if you count the grass-like trio as one. The last group is the old lily family: monocots (lesson 21) with flower parts in threes or sixes, parallel-veined leaves, and often a bulb. DNA has split it into several families. True lilies and tulips stay in the lily family. Irises have a family of their own, onions and daffodils are in another, and camas, like asparagus, is in the asparagus family.[^lily-split] In the field the old signature still works for recognising a lily-like monocot; the family name tells you which branch it is on.

Take this lesson's signatures to a garden centre or a vegetable stall, where the plants are labelled. Find a member of each family and check its signature: roll a mint stem, find the keel in a pea flower, count a mustard's petals and long stamens, look at a carrot's umbel and a lettuce gone to flower. Then try the same on a walk, where nothing is labelled.

blocks.caption: Six questions on families
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A plant has a square stem, opposite leaves and two-lipped flowers, and smells when a leaf is crushed. Which family?
items.why: Square stems, opposite leaves and two-lipped flowers are the mint family's signature.

items.ask: A plant has tiny white flowers on spokes like an umbrella, and hollow stems. Which family?
items.why: Umbels on hollow stems mark the carrot family, which holds both parsley and some of the most poisonous plants there are.

choices: A head of hundreds of tiny flowers
A flower with an unusually large centre
items.why: In the aster family, each tiny flower in the disc makes one seed, and the flowers round the edge each grow one long petal.

items.ask: A flower has four petals in a cross and six stamens, four long and two short. Which family?
items.why: The cross gave the mustard family its old name, Cruciferae.

items.ask: A grass-like plant in a wet meadow has a solid stem with three sharp edges. What is it?
items.why: Sedges have edges; rushes are round and solid; grasses are round and hollow with joints.

items.ask: Why is a family's signature more reliable than any one feature?
choices: Many unrelated plants share one feature, but few share the whole set
A signature is always visible, even without flowers
items.why: Five petals alone says little. Five petals, many stamens, toothed leaves and leaf-base flaps together say rose family.

summary: **Know the family first.** A family's own key is far shorter than a key to everything.
**A signature is a few features together.** No one feature is enough.
**Rose, pea, mint, aster, carrot, mustard, buttercup and heath** each have a flower or growth habit you can learn at a glance.
**Sedges have edges, rushes are round, grasses have joints.** Roll the stem between your fingers.
**Grasses feed the world.** Wheat, rice and corn are grasses; their tiny green flowers are pollinated by wind.
**The old lily family is now several.** Lilies, irises, onions and camas sit in different families, but the lily-like signature still spots them.

orchids.title: The other giant family
orchids.text: The other of the two largest families is the orchids, Orchidaceae, with nearly 30,000 species of its own. Most orchids live in the tropics, often perched on tree branches rather than rooted in soil, so in a temperate meadow the aster family has far more representatives.

old-names.title: Latin family names
old-names.text: Modern botanical Latin gives every family a name ending in *-aceae*, built from a genus in that family: Rosaceae from *Rosa*, Asteraceae from *Aster*, Brassicaceae (mustards) from *Brassica*. Eight families also keep older descriptive names that are still legal to use, because they are so common in older books: Cruciferae (cross-bearers, the mustards), Leguminosae (pod-bearers, the peas), Labiatae (lipped flowers, the mints), Compositae (compound heads, the asters), Umbelliferae (umbrella-bearers, the carrots), Gramineae (the grasses), Palmae (the palms) and Guttiferae (Saint John's wort's relatives).

lily-split.title: What happened to the lily family
lily-split.text: Irises, with three stamens rather than six, have long had their own family (Iridaceae). Onions, daffodils and camas were often kept inside a broad lily family (Liliaceae) in older field guides. DNA evidence showed that the three-petalled, six-stamened bulb habit evolved more than once or was kept by cousins that branched apart early, so botanists moved onions and daffodils into Amaryllidaceae and camas into Asparagaceae.
